questions.question: Which of the following alkenes exists as cis and trans isomers?

solution.key_concept: Geometrical isomerism requires each doubly bonded carbon to carry two different groups.
steps: In propene ($CH_3CH=CH_2$), the terminal carbon carries two H atoms, so it shows no isomerism.
In but-1-ene ($CH_3CH_2CH=CH_2$), the terminal carbon also carries two H atoms.
In ethene, both carbons carry two H atoms.
In but-2-ene ($CH_3CH=CHCH_3$), each carbon carries H and $CH_3$, so cis and trans forms exist.
solution.why_not_others: Propene, but-1-ene and ethene each have at least one carbon bearing two identical H atoms.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that every alkene with four or more carbons shows cis-trans isomerism. But-1-ene does not.
solution.time_saving_tip: Look for a $=CH_2$ end. If one is present, the alkene cannot show geometrical isomerism.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene?
options: trans-But-2-ene has the higher boiling point because it is more stable
cis-But-2-ene has zero dipole moment because its methyl groups are on the same side
cis-But-2-ene has the higher melting point because it packs better in the crystal lattice
cis-But-2-ene has the higher boiling point, while trans-but-2-ene has the higher melting point

solution.key_concept: Cis isomers are more polar and have higher boiling points. Trans isomers pack better and have higher melting points.
steps: cis-But-2-ene boils at about 277 K and trans-but-2-ene at about 274 K, so the cis isomer has the higher boiling point.
trans-But-2-ene has zero dipole moment, so the cis isomer is the more polar one.
The trans isomer packs better in the crystal lattice, so it has the higher melting point.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): cis-But-2-ene has the higher boiling point, while trans-but-2-ene has the higher melting point
solution.why_not_others: (1) The boiling point order is reversed. (2) It is the trans isomer that has zero dipole moment. (3) Better packing is a property of the trans isomer.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that the more stable trans isomer must have the higher boiling point as well as the higher melting point.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember: cis gives higher b.p. (polarity); trans gives higher m.p. (packing).

questions.question: But-2-yne is reduced in two separate experiments: with $H_2$/Lindlar's catalyst to give P, and with $Na$/liquid $NH_3$ to give Q. Which statement is correct?
options: P has a higher boiling point than Q, and P and Q are diastereomers
P and Q are enantiomers with identical boiling points
Q has a higher dipole moment than P
P and Q are identical compounds

solution.key_concept: Lindlar's catalyst gives the cis alkene and $Na$/liquid $NH_3$ gives the trans alkene. Geometrical isomers are diastereomers.
steps: P is cis-but-2-ene and Q is trans-but-2-ene.
Geometrical isomers are diastereomers and have different physical properties.
The cis isomer is more polar and boils higher (about 277 K versus 274 K).
solution.final_answer: Option (1): P has a higher boiling point than Q, and P and Q are diastereomers
solution.why_not_others: (2) Geometrical isomers are not enantiomers, and their boiling points differ. (3) Q (trans) has zero dipole moment. (4) The two reagents give different stereoisomers.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up which reagent gives which isomer, or calling cis and trans isomers enantiomers.
solution.time_saving_tip: Lindlar gives cis; Na/liq. $NH_3$ gives trans.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: But-1-ene does not show geometrical isomerism.
statements.R: Interconversion of cis and trans isomers of an alkene requires breaking of the pi bond, for example by heat or light.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Geometrical isomerism needs two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon.
steps: In but-1-ene, $C$-1 carries two H atoms, so geometrical isomerism is not possible. A is true.
Cis-trans interconversion requires breaking the pi bond by heat or light. R is true.
A is explained by the two identical H atoms on $C$-1, not by the energy needed to interconvert isomers.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: R is a correct fact, but it explains why geometrical isomers are stable and separable. It does not explain why but-1-ene lacks such isomers.
solution.common_trap: Selecting option (1) simply because both statements concern geometrical isomerism.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: 2-Methylbut-2-ene, $(CH_3)_2C=CHCH_3$, exists as cis and trans isomers because rotation about the $C=C$ bond is restricted.
statements.II: 1-Chloropropene, $ClCH=CHCH_3$, shows geometrical isomerism because each doubly bonded carbon carries two different groups.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Restricted rotation is necessary but not sufficient. Each doubly bonded carbon must also carry two different groups.
steps: In 2-methylbut-2-ene, $C$-2 carries two identical $CH_3$ groups, so there are no cis-trans isomers. Statement I is incorrect.
In 1-chloropropene, $C$-1 carries Cl and H, and $C$-2 carries $CH_3$ and H.
Both carbons carry two different groups, so cis and trans forms exist. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I fails the condition $a \neq b$ on one carbon. Statement II satisfies it on both carbons.
solution.common_trap: Treating restricted rotation alone as enough for geometrical isomerism.
solution.time_saving_tip: Check each $sp^2$ carbon separately for two identical substituents.

questions.question: Ethene gas is bubbled through a solution of bromine in $CCl_4$. Which observation, with the correct product, indicates the presence of the double bond?
options: The red-brown colour deepens, and bromoethane is formed
A white precipitate appears, and ethyne is formed
The red-brown colour is discharged, and 1,2-dibromoethane is formed
The solution turns purple, and ethane-1,2-diol is formed

solution.key_concept: Decolourisation of red-brown $Br_2$ in $CCl_4$ is a test for unsaturation.
steps: $Br_2$ adds across the $C=C$ bond: $CH_2=CH_2 + Br_2 \rightarrow BrCH_2CH_2Br$.
As the bromine is consumed, its red-brown colour disappears.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): The red-brown colour is discharged, and 1,2-dibromoethane is formed
solution.why_not_others: Bromine is consumed, so the colour cannot deepen. Addition of $Br_2$ gives a dibromide, not bromoethane, ethyne or a diol, and no precipitate or purple colour forms.
solution.common_trap: Confusing this test with the $KMnO_4$ test or the test for terminal alkynes.

questions.question: trans-But-2-ene reacts with $Br_2$ in $CCl_4$. What is the product?
options: A mixture of cis- and trans-2,3-dibromobut-2-ene

solution.key_concept: Bromine adds anti through a cyclic bromonium ion.
steps: $Br_2$ forms a cyclic bromonium ion on one face of the alkene.
$Br^-$ then attacks from the opposite face, so the overall addition is anti.
Anti addition to a trans-alkene gives the meso dibromide.
solution.why_not_others: (1) The racemic product comes from cis-but-2-ene. (2) Addition saturates the double bond, so no alkene remains. (3) The bromine atoms add to $C$-2 and $C$-3, not to $C$-1 and $C$-2.
solution.common_trap: Assuming syn addition of $Br_2$, which would wrongly predict the racemic product.
solution.time_saving_tip: For anti addition, remember 'trans gives meso, cis gives racemic'.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of reactivity of hydrogen halides towards addition to an alkene?

solution.key_concept: HX reactivity follows H–X bond weakness.
steps: The first step is transfer of $H^+$ to the alkene, which is the rate-determining step.
The weaker the H–X bond, the more easily $H^+$ is transferred.
Bond strength decreases from HCl to HI, so reactivity is $HI > HBr > HCl$.
solution.why_not_others: (1) and (4) reverse the true order. (3) wrongly places HBr above HI, probably because HBr is the reagent linked with the peroxide effect.
solution.common_trap: Arranging the hydrogen halides by electronegativity of the halogen instead of by bond weakness.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

solution.key_concept: $Br_2$ adds anti, cold alkaline $KMnO_4$ adds syn, and acid-catalysed hydration follows Markovnikov's rule.
steps: A: anti addition to a cis-alkene gives the racemic dibromide (II).
B: anti addition to a trans-alkene gives the meso dibromide (I).
C: syn addition to a cis-alkene gives the meso diol (III).
D: Markovnikov hydration of propene gives $CH_3CH(OH)CH_3$, propan-2-ol (IV).
solution.why_not_others: Options (1) and (3) treat $Br_2$ addition as syn. Options (2) and (3) mix up the diol and the alcohol products.
solution.common_trap: Treating every addition as anti, or every addition as syn.
solution.time_saving_tip: Fix D first (propan-2-ol). That leaves only options (1) and (4), which differ in the $Br_2$ matches.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about electrophilic addition to alkenes are correct?

statements.A: Catalytic hydrogenation over $Pt$, $Pd$ or $Ni$ occurs by syn addition on the metal surface.
statements.B: In the addition of $HBr$, attack of $Br^-$ on the carbocation is the rate-determining step.
statements.C: Acid-catalysed hydration of propene gives propan-2-ol.
statements.D: Acid-catalysed hydration of ethene gives a secondary alcohol.
statements.E: Bromination proceeds through a cyclic bromonium ion that is attacked by $Br^-$ from the opposite face.

options: A, C, D and E only

solution.key_concept: Mechanistic details of hydrogenation, HX addition, hydration and halogenation.
steps: A is correct: hydrogenation on the metal surface is syn.
B is incorrect: addition of $H^+$ to form the carbocation is the rate-determining step.
C is correct: Markovnikov hydration of propene gives $CH_3CH(OH)CH_3$.
D is incorrect: ethene gives ethanol, a primary alcohol.
E is correct: bromination proceeds through a bromonium ion with anti attack by $Br^-$.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) includes B, which names the wrong slow step. Options (3) and (4) include D, but ethene gives a primary alcohol.
solution.common_trap: Generalising 'hydration gives $2^\circ$ or $3^\circ$ alcohols' to ethene.

questions.question: What is the major product of the reaction of propene with $HBr$ in the absence of peroxide?

solution.key_concept: Markovnikov's rule: the negative part of the reagent adds to the carbon carrying fewer hydrogens.
steps: $H^+$ adds to the terminal carbon to give the more stable $2^\circ$ carbocation, $CH_3\overset{+}{C}HCH_3$.
$Br^-$ attacks this cation to give $CH_3CHBrCH_3$.
solution.why_not_others: (1) 1-Bromopropane forms only with peroxide. (2) 1,2-Dibromopropane is the $Br_2$ addition product. (3) Propan-2-ol is the hydration product.
solution.common_trap: Applying the peroxide effect when no peroxide is present.

questions.question: In the presence of benzoyl peroxide, which hydrogen halide adds to propene in the anti-Markovnikov manner?

solution.key_concept: The peroxide (Kharasch) effect is shown only by $HBr$.
steps: The H–Cl bond is too strong to be cleaved by radicals, so HCl shows no peroxide effect.
The H–I bond breaks easily, but iodine radicals combine to form $I_2$ instead of adding to the alkene.
Only $Br^\bullet$ adds to the double bond, so only HBr gives the anti-Markovnikov product.
solution.why_not_others: Each of options (2), (3) and (4) includes HCl or HI, neither of which shows the peroxide effect.
solution.common_trap: Extending the peroxide effect to all hydrogen halides.

questions.question: What is the major product of the reaction of $C_6H_5-CH=CH-CH_3$ with $HBr$ in the presence of benzoyl peroxide?

solution.key_concept: With peroxide, $Br^\bullet$ adds so as to give the more stable carbon radical. For this alkene, the more stable radical is benzylic.
steps: $Br^\bullet$ adds to the carbon next to $CH_3$, leaving a benzylic radical on the carbon attached to the ring.
This radical abstracts H from HBr.
Br ends up on the carbon next to $CH_3$: $C_6H_5CH_2CHBrCH_3$.
solution.why_not_others: (1) is the ionic product, formed without peroxide, with Br on the benzylic carbon. (3) puts Br on a carbon that was not part of the double bond. (4) is a dibromide, which comes from $Br_2$ addition.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that the products with and without peroxide are stereoisomers. They are position isomers.
solution.time_saving_tip: Ionic addition puts Br where the stable cation forms. Radical addition puts Br on the other carbon, leaving the stable radical behind.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Propene reacts with $HCl$ in the presence of benzoyl peroxide to give 1-chloropropane as the major product.
statements.R: In the presence of peroxides, $HBr$ adds to propene by a free radical mechanism in which $Br^\bullet$ adds to the terminal carbon.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: The peroxide effect is limited to HBr.
steps: The H–Cl bond is too strong to be cleaved by radicals, so HCl adds by the Markovnikov route and gives 2-chloropropane. A is false.
With peroxide, HBr adds by a radical mechanism in which $Br^\bullet$ adds to the terminal carbon to give the more stable radical. R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so options (1), (2) and (3) are all ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Assuming HCl behaves like HBr in the presence of peroxides.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Both the Markovnikov and the anti-Markovnikov additions of $HBr$ to propene proceed through the more stable intermediate; they differ only in the attacking species ($H^+$ versus $Br^\bullet$).
statements.II: $HI$ does not show the peroxide effect, even though the H–I bond is weak, because iodine radicals combine to form $I_2$ rather than add to the double bond.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Orientation is controlled by the stability of the intermediate: the carbocation in ionic addition and the radical in peroxide-initiated addition.
steps: Ionic addition: $H^+$ attacks first to give the $2^\circ$ carbocation. Radical addition: $Br^\bullet$ attacks first to give the $2^\circ$ radical. Statement I is correct.
The H–I bond breaks easily, but $I^\bullet$ radicals combine to form $I_2$. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements match the mechanism exactly.
solution.common_trap: Believing that HI fails to show the peroxide effect because its bond is too strong. That is the reason for HCl, not HI.

questions.question: What does but-2-ene give on ozonolysis followed by treatment with $Zn$/$H_2O$?

solution.key_concept: Each $C=C$ is replaced by two $C=O$ groups. A symmetrical alkene gives a single carbonyl product.
steps: Cleaving $CH_3CH=CHCH_3$ at the double bond gives $CH_3CH=O$ from each half.
The product is two molecules of ethanal.
solution.why_not_others: (1) is the product set of but-1-ene. (3) is the product set of 2-methylpropene. (4) does not form, because $Zn$ prevents oxidation of aldehydes to acids.
solution.common_trap: Writing carboxylic acids as products and forgetting the role of $Zn$.

questions.question: An alkene gives propanone and ethanal on reductive ozonolysis. Which alkene is it?

solution.key_concept: Join the carbonyl carbons of the products with a double bond to rebuild the alkene.
steps: Propanone is $(CH_3)_2C=O$ and ethanal is $CH_3CH=O$.
Replacing the two $C=O$ groups with one $C=C$ gives $(CH_3)_2C=CHCH_3$.
This alkene is 2-methylbut-2-ene.
solution.why_not_others: (1) gives butanone and methanal. (2) gives ethanal and propanal. (4) gives 2-methylpropanal and methanal.
solution.common_trap: Matching only the carbon count ($C_5$) and ignoring where the double bond is.
solution.time_saving_tip: A ketone product means one alkene carbon is $=CR_2$.

questions.question: An alkene of formula $C_6H_{12}$ gives a single carbonyl compound, a ketone, on ozonolysis followed by $Zn$/$H_2O$. Which alkene is it?

solution.key_concept: A symmetrical alkene gives one product. A ketone forms only from a $=CR_2$ carbon.
steps: A single product means the alkene is symmetrical. Carbon is conserved, so each half has 3 carbons.
For the product to be a ketone, each alkene carbon must be $=C(CH_3)_2$.
The alkene is $(CH_3)_2C=C(CH_3)_2$, which gives 2 molecules of propanone.
solution.why_not_others: (1) gives a single product, but it is propanal, an aldehyde. (2) gives propanone and propanal. (4) gives 2,2-dimethylpropanal and methanal.
solution.common_trap: Choosing hex-3-ene because it is also symmetrical, without checking whether the product is a ketone.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

solution.key_concept: In reductive ozonolysis, terminal $=CH_2$ gives $HCHO$, $=CHR$ gives $RCHO$, and $=CR_2$ gives a ketone.
steps: A: $CH_3CH=CH_2$ gives $CH_3CHO + HCHO$ (II).
B: $CH_2=CH_2$ gives only $HCHO$ (I).
C: $(CH_3)_2C=CH_2$ gives $(CH_3)_2CO + HCHO$ (III).
D: $CH_3CH_2CH=CH_2$ gives $CH_3CH_2CHO + HCHO$ (IV).
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) gives ethene two different products. Option (3) assigns an aldehyde to 2-methylpropene. Option (4) mismatches the carbon counts of propene and but-1-ene.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting that a symmetrical alkene gives only one carbonyl compound.
solution.time_saving_tip: Check that the carbons in the products add up to the carbons in the alkene.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about ozonolysis and polymerisation of alkenes are correct?

statements.A: In reductive ozonolysis, each $C=C$ bond is replaced by two $C=O$ groups.
statements.B: The repeat unit of polypropene, $-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-$, has the same molecular formula as the monomer.
statements.C: Reductive ozonolysis of 2-methylpropene gives two different aldehydes.
statements.D: Polymerisation of ethene can be carried out at high temperature and pressure with a trace of $O_2$ or a peroxide initiator, or with a Ziegler-Natta catalyst.
statements.E: In reductive ozonolysis, the total number of carbon atoms in the carbonyl products exceeds that in the alkene.

options: A, B, C and D only

solution.key_concept: Facts about reductive ozonolysis and addition polymerisation.
steps: A is correct: each $C=C$ becomes two $C=O$ groups.
B is correct: in addition polymers, the repeat unit has the same formula as the monomer.
C is incorrect: 2-methylpropene gives propanone (a ketone) and methanal.
D is correct: these are the stated conditions for polymerising ethene.
E is incorrect: the number of carbons is conserved in reductive ozonolysis.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, B and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) includes C, which is false. Option (2) leaves out the true statement B. Option (3) includes the false statements C and E.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting that a $=CR_2$ carbon gives a ketone, not an aldehyde.
